content: Cervical dilatation and uterine interventions are procedures that can be performed using sedation, local anesthesia, or general anesthesia, particularly in the context of obstetric and gynecological conditions. Paracervical local anesthesia (PLA) is commonly used by gynecologists, but its effectiveness remains uncertain. This review, originally published in 2009 and updated in 2013, aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of PLA compared to no treatment, placebo, other regional anesthesia methods, sedation, systemic analgesia, or general anesthesia. The search for relevant studies was conducted up to August 2013, including databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as reference lists of articles. The original search was performed in January 2006. The review included randomized or controlled clinical trials involving women undergoing cervical dilatation and uterine interventions. Studies comparing PLA with no treatment, placebo, other regional anesthesia methods, systemic sedation and analgesia, or general anesthesia were included. Two authors independently assessed the studies, extracted data, and entered the information into Review Manager. This updated review incorporated nine new studies, resulting in a total of 26 studies with 28 comparisons and 2,790 participants. However, no study comparing PLA to general anesthesia met the inclusion criteria. Ten studies compared PLA to placebo. PLA was found to reduce pain during cervical dilatation, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.37 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.58) and a relative risk (RR) of severe pain of 0.16 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.74). PLA also reduced abdominal pain during uterine interventions (SMD 0.74, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.19), but it had no effect on postoperative back or shoulder pain. Comparisons of PLA to no treatment did not demonstrate any significant effect. Five studies compared PLA to other regional anesthesia techniques, such as uterosacral block, intracervical block, or intrauterine topical anesthesia. Two of these studies found no significant difference in pain during the procedure. When compared to intrauterine instillation, PLA slightly reduced severe pain (from 8.3 to 7.6 on a 10-point scale), but this reduction may be clinically negligible. Six studies compared PLA to sedation. There were no statistically significant differences in pain during or after the procedure, postoperative analgesia requirements, adverse effects, patient satisfaction, or the operator's perception of analgesia. The risk of bias was assessed using six domains, and more than half of the included studies were found to have a low risk of bias. The authors concluded that no analgesic technique provided reliable pain control in the 26 included studies. Some studies reported that women experienced severe pain (mean scores of 7 to 9 out of 10) during uterine interventions, regardless of the analgesic technique used. The available evidence does not demonstrate whether PLA is inferior, equivalent, or superior to alternative analgesic techniques in terms of efficacy and safety for women undergoing cervical dilatation and uterine interventions. The authors suggest that women are likely to find the pain experienced during uterine interventions performed without neuraxial blockade to be unacceptable, and this pain is not significantly altered by the use of PLA.
